Reviews · TVR Sagaris

The Assassin

It wasn’t designed to impress you. It was designed to destroy your expectations. 400 horsepower from 6 cylinders, a body shaped by racing and an attitude that bordered on criminal: the TVR Sagaris was the ultimate expression of Blackpool’s rebellion, and tragically, it arrived just in time to say goodbye.

By Diana Chambers · 18 minute read

406 bhp
From TVR’s own 4.0-liter straight-six
377

3.7 sec

Some cars are beautiful. Others are fast. A select few manage to be both. And then there are cars that look as though someone has already committed a terrible act of violence with them and is simply waiting for the next opportunity. Welcome to the TVR Sagaris.

There is nothing remotely apologetic about this car. Look at the front end. The headlights appear to have been carved into the body with a knife, the hood is covered in openings and sculpted channels, and the front fenders are slashed with vents that look like scars. The wheel arches bulge over enormous tires, the roofline sits impossibly low, and the whole machine seems to crouch in anticipation of something unpleasant.

Walk around the back and things don’t improve. There is a sharply cut tail, a spoiler standing on a pair of polished metal fins, muscular rear arches and exhausts that leave sideways out of the corners, as though positioned without the slightest concern for social convention. The Sagaris doesn’t look as though it wants to race you. It looks as though it already knows the outcome, and that is precisely what makes it so extraordinary.

Every TVR in this family had a character. The Griffith was the hot rod, muscular and charismatic, with a wonderful disregard for moderation. The Chimaera was the gentleman spy on holiday, elegant and dangerous when required. The Cerbera was the family man with a criminal record, the Tamora the weekend escape artist who preferred a good road to an audience, and the Tuscan the showman, flamboyant and impossible to ignore. The Sagaris was the assassin. It’s here for one thing, and you’re it.

The briefWhen outrageous was no longer outrageous enough

By the early 2000s, TVR had already built the Griffith, the Chimaera, the Cerbera and the Tuscan, and the Tamora and the T350 coupe built on it had shown it could make a balanced, predictable car without losing the excitement. So where could it possibly go next? More power, stranger styling, a lower roof, bigger wheels and more aerodynamic parts? Naturally, the answer was all of the above.

But the Sagaris was more purposeful than another exercise in outrageousness, and the name says so. A sagaris was the battle-ax of the horse-riding Scythian warriors of the ancient steppe, a long-shafted weapon with a blade on one side and a spike on the other. The Tamora was named after a vengeful queen. The Sagaris was named after the thing she would have hired someone to use.

Its real roots were in racing. In 2003, TVR took 2 T400R race cars, developed from the T350, to Le Mans, and neither finished. The design team, led by Graham Browne, came home, took the T350 coupe as its base and added a whole arsenal of spoilers, winglets and other aerodynamic aids to pin the car to the road at speed. TVR’s reasoning was that racing rules would limit how much the race cars could be changed, so the road car had to carry its aerodynamic advantages from the factory, with a front splitter and rear diffuser built into the body. It was, in the company’s own words, “designed to sit as low as TVR dares.”

And because it was TVR, subtlety was discarded immediately. The first Sagaris, a gray prototype, appeared on December 11, 2003, in the Live Action Arena on the opening day of the MPH Show at London’s Earls Court. It looked as though someone had handed a T350 to a racing engineer with a vivid imagination and told him to remove anything that might be considered unnecessary restraint. Soon afterward, evo’s John Barker had the show car out on the road beside a Griffith 400 and a 450 SEAC, TVR’s past lined up next to its future.

The lookStyling by blunt force trauma

The Sagaris challenges the idea that a car must be beautiful in the conventional sense, and yet I find it absolutely stunning. Not the way I admire the Cerbera’s elegant profile, or the way the Chimaera’s curves seem to grow more attractive with age. The Sagaris is beautiful because it is so unashamedly purposeful. It looks like a weapon, and almost every styling element reinforces the impression. The front end is dominated by deeply recessed headlights, an aggressive lower air intake and a hood that seems to have been sculpted around the needs of the engine and its cooling rather than the preferences of a marketing department.

Then there are the vents. Oh, those vents. Slashes run across the tops of the front fenders, as if the bodywork had been cut open to release something trapped beneath, and they earned the car a nickname: the axe murderer. The arches are dramatically flared, the profile is low and muscular, and the cabin sits well back, with a compact tail rising abruptly behind it. Where the Cerbera and Tuscan flow gracefully down into their rear bumpers, the Sagaris’s bodywork ends with an almost brutal abruptness. There is nothing delicate about it, and that is exactly why it works. It isn’t trying to be a grand tourer, to look expensive or even to seem sophisticated. It wants you to understand that this is a serious performance machine, and it makes that point before the engine has even started.

The aeroThe difference between aggression and purpose

What separates the Sagaris from the many modern cars that rely on aggressive styling for a personality is that its looks were not merely theater. The front splitter managed the air beneath the car. The rear diffuser and the Gurney flap on the tail managed the air leaving it. The slashes above the front wheels were originally open, giving an escape route to the hot, high-pressure air building up under the hood and over the splitter, and the exhausts point sideways because that layout kept back pressure down. On the prototype, the rear valance wrapped almost completely around them, and the vents in the hood opened and closed on electric actuators.

Then real-world testing intervened. The open slashes flung road dirt and plumes of water from the front wheels all over the hood and windshield, which is not ideal in a vehicle meant for public roads, and they were expensive to make. So by the time the first 2 pre-production cars appeared at the NEC Motor Show in Birmingham in May 2004, the slashes had been filled in. The actuator-driven hood vents became simpler manual ones to save money, and the rear valance was cut back from the exhausts to keep heat out of the body. It is one of my favorite details about the car, because it captures TVR perfectly: racing ambition, meeting the realities of a road car. The central idea survived intact. The Sagaris would look and feel as close to a racing car as TVR could make it while still wearing license plates.

The platformThe T350 that went to war

Beneath the bodywork was a familiar foundation, and this is where the engineering story gets interesting. The T350 had grown out of the Tamora, keeping much of its running gear but adding a stiff coupe body, and testers praised it for its precision, balance and predictability. TVR was learning that extraordinary performance didn’t have to come with unpredictable handling, and that was exactly the foundation the Sagaris needed.

It wasn’t simply a T350 in an extravagant body kit. The Sagaris was 65 mm (2.6 in) wider than the T350, and in a light sports car, changes to track width, wheels, tires and suspension geometry transform the way it behaves. The wider footprint brought more stability and room for much bigger tires, 255/35 R18s on 18-inch, 7-spoke wheels at all 4 corners, with double-wishbone suspension and a Hydratrak limited-slip differential to put the power down. The most important change, though, wasn’t one you could see. It was the way the car drove.

The numbers400 horsepower. No excuses.

Specifications from TVR’s 2005 Sagaris press release. Ralph Dodds’s book quotes 400 bhp, 270 lb-ft and 195 mph, and independent test results can differ from factory claims. Production: PistonHeads. Dollars at 2004’s average exchange rate (about $1.83 to the pound); 2026 figures use UK consumer price inflation (in2013dollars) and about $1.33 to the pound.

Put those figures in perspective. When the Sagaris arrived, 400 horsepower was still a serious achievement for any sports car, let alone one TVR said weighed 1,078 kg (2,377 lb). Ferrari’s new F430 had 490 PS (483 hp) but carried far more weight. Porsche’s 996 GT3 RS had 381 PS (376 hp), and BMW’s M3 CSL 360 PS (355 hp). On TVR’s figures, the Sagaris carried 377 bhp for every 1,000 kg (2,205 lb), and even if you add the 100 kg (220 lb) one magazine found on a test car with air conditioning, it still beats the Porsche and the Ferrari. Then consider the price. At £49,995 ($91,600), about £99,600 ($132,100) in 2026 money, it cost less than 60 percent of a GT3 RS and less than half an F430. It wasn’t merely quick for a TVR. It was quick by any standard.

TVR claimed 0–60 mph in 3.7 seconds and 100 mph in 8.1, figures that remain impressive today, but as with the Cerbera, the real story was what happened beyond 60. In the gears, Dodds reports, 30 to 70 mph took just 3 seconds, the kind of number that ends an argument on a 2-lane road before it starts, and Autocar’s testers recorded 150 mph from a standstill in 20.0 seconds. One published road test, timed from a standstill, took it through the quarter mile in 12.7 seconds, crossing the line at 122 mph. Car and Driver’s Ferrari F430 crossed it at 123.

None of it needed launch control or a clever automatic gearbox, just displacement, revs, low weight and a driver who knew what he was doing, joined by something many modern cars have lost: a direct line between the driver’s actions and the machine’s response. There was no traction control, no stability control, no electronically controlled differential redistributing the power and no ABS. If the driver made a mistake, the car was not necessarily going to correct it. That made the Sagaris thrilling and demanding in equal measure, and that is exactly what its customers wanted.

The voiceThe engine that refused to die

The Sagaris used TVR’s 4.0-liter Speed Six in one of its most powerful production forms, the same all-aluminum, dry-sump straight-six with twin overhead camshafts and 4 valves per cylinder that had powered the Cerbera Speed Six, the Tuscan and the T350, and the engine whose early troubles nearly broke the company, as the Tuscan’s story tells. By the time the Sagaris arrived, years of revised parts and materials had made this one of the most developed versions of it.

It was also central to the car’s character. Where a turbocharged engine delivers one broad, effortless surge, the Speed Six rewarded revs, its power building to a harder and more urgent mechanical howl, more competition engine than road car. There was something almost theatrical in the partnership. The car looked angry, and the engine sounded as though it agreed.

The chassisThe real weapon was the chassis

This is where the Sagaris becomes more than another outrageously fast TVR, because TVR had been building those for years. Horsepower alone was never going to make it the company’s greatest achievement. Its reputation arrived first. Dodds calls the Tamora and T350 the tamed TVRs, cars that gave drivers time to fix their mistakes, and writes that the car they spawned was “just waiting to amplify the driver’s slightest error.” But imagine approaching a fast corner in a powerful rear-wheel-drive car. You brake and let the weight move forward, turn the wheel and wait for the front tires to respond, and in many cars there is a moment of doubt about whether the nose will bite and the tail will follow. The Sagaris was developed to remove that doubt. Its electro-hydraulic steering needed only 2 turns from lock to lock, and it communicated clearly. The nose responded decisively, the suspension held the body in check, and the extra width gave the car a stability no TVR had had before. Where you might expect a 400 bhp TVR to grow nervous, the Sagaris settles and tightens, and the faster you go, the calmer it becomes.

That was deliberate. Rather than build the car around the dramatic oversteer of some earlier TVRs, the engineers gave it a mild understeer at speed. That might disappoint anyone who thinks every serious sports car should be permanently sideways, but a car with 400 horsepower, very little weight and no stability control does not need encouraging. It needs a chassis that lets the driver choose what happens, and with the Hydratrak differential, a skilled driver could still bring the tail around on the throttle and hold it there. The brakes, without ABS, were fierce and full of feel, but overdo them and the front wheels lock, so you squeeze, release and squeeze again, the way drivers did before computers did it for them. The assassin doesn’t waste movement. It doesn’t need unnecessary gestures, only precision, control and the ability to finish the job, and Autocar summed it up in 5 words: “The best TVR in history.”

The cockpitThe extraordinary feeling of simply being inside one

Approach a Sagaris and the roof barely reaches your waist; the whole car stands just 1,175 mm (46.3 in) tall. You open the door, there is no handle to pull, the release is electric, and you lower yourself into the seat. Lower is the right word. You don’t sit down in a Sagaris. You descend into it, into a TVR-made racing seat beneath the bars of a roll cage built to FIA rules and welded into the chassis, with the transmission tunnel rising beside you and the long hood stretching ahead, its sculpted vents visible through the windshield.

Yet it isn’t stripped bare. TVR knew buyers at this price still wanted the trappings of lesser cars, so every Sagaris came trimmed in full leather hide, with machined aluminum details, a polished aluminum gear lever and handbrake, and programmable digital instruments. Air conditioning was a £1,930 ($3,500) option, about £3,800 ($5,100) today, and most buyers ticked the box. There is even a genuinely useful trunk behind you, 495 liters (17.5 cu ft) by PistonHeads’ measure. Luxury was never the point, though. The sense of occasion was.

Getting out again is its own ceremony. The door opens from a button on the dash beside the radio, conventional by TVR’s standards, and climbing out of something so low takes a little thought, as it does in a Lotus Exige. I suspect owners rather enjoyed that, because it reinforces the feeling that this is no ordinary car. Outside, the Sagaris looks ready to attack everything in sight. Inside, it is leather and a very British idea of sporting luxury: not a racing car with license plates, but a road car built to be driven hard.

The one TVR never got to finish

A test bed. TVR Car Club regional organizer Tim Payne bought his Sagaris in 2008. Sold new in 2005 in iced titanium gray and now painted in a color called copper cascade, it has become a rolling record of what TVR meant to do before time ran out, with much of the work done by former TVR employees.

The original plan. Its fender vents have been opened up as the first design intended, and it finally has the automatic, actuator-driven hood vents TVR gave up on after too many technical problems.

The unfinished business. The engine has been upgraded to the more reliable Super Sport specification, and its engine-management chip now carries the features TVR was still developing when it went under in 2006, launch control among them.

The last jobThe company that built its best car just before disappearing

And now we arrive at the part of the story I find genuinely heartbreaking. The Sagaris should have been the beginning of something extraordinary. It brought together better chassis development, more mature aerodynamics, a further-developed engine and arguably the most spectacular body TVR ever produced, and for the first time, TVR’s cars were praised for the quality of the whole driving experience, not just their speed and personality. Instead, it became one of the last great achievements of the original TVR in Blackpool.

Just as TVR reached that point, its future slipped away. As soon as the May 2004 NEC show was over, rumors spread around the Bristol Avenue factory that Peter Wheeler had put the company up for sale, and on July 27, 2004, TVR announced it had been sold to Nikolai Smolenski, a young Russian banker, who promised investment, modernization and better production quality. Wheeler stayed on as a consultant. The new owner tightened quality control to fight TVR’s reputation for unreliability, which pushed the first deliveries back to the end of 2004, and the cars built in 2005 and 2006 were the finest TVR ever made. PistonHeads calls the Sagaris the “best-built TVR ever.”

It wasn’t enough. The Speed Six’s reputation had scared buyers away, warranty costs had been heavy, production was expensive, and customers were growing used to the safety aids and reliability of the big manufacturers. Priced to match the Tuscan S, the Sagaris drew a steady stream of deposits even as the order book thinned, but nothing like the floods that had greeted the Griffith and the Tuscan, and only 211 had been built when the Blackpool factory closed in December 2006. Peter Wheeler died on June 11, 2009, after a long illness, a year after TVR’s founder, Trevor Wilkinson.

The questionWas this the best possible way to go out?

There is an uncomfortable question here. If a manufacturer is destined to disappear, is it better to fade away slowly, building ever more compromised cars to survive, or to leave behind something extraordinary? I would rather TVR had survived. Imagine a further-developed Sagaris with a more dependable engine and better build quality, a genuine rival to the 911 GT3 and every new Corvette. TVR had the imagination and the engineering. What it lacked was the money to do it consistently. But there is another way to see the ending. TVR didn’t close its Blackpool era with a forgettable car or a safer formula that abandoned its identity. One of its final creations was arguably the most aggressive, the most visually extraordinary and the most dynamically accomplished car it ever built: a 400 horsepower, naturally aspirated, manual, rear-wheel-drive sports car with almost no electronic help and a body designed to terrify the competition. If TVR had to take its final bow, it chose a spectacular outfit, and it delivered one hell of a performance.

The presenceMore than 20 years later, it still looks angry

Some cars date almost immediately, and others, like the Jaguar E-Type and the original Porsche 911, become timeless. The Sagaris doesn’t look timeless in the traditional sense. It looks as though time has simply failed to catch up with it. Park one beside a modern supercar with twice the power and far more technology, and ask which looks more exciting, more purposeful, more extraordinary. I don’t think it’s the new one. The knife-cut headlights, slashed fenders, huge arches and truncated tail still look almost futuristic, and the Sagaris manages it without the enormous size modern cars rely on. Its aggression comes from its proportions and details, so it looks concentrated, as though every inch of it exists to serve the performance.

That is why it draws more attention than ice in the desert. Pull into a gas station and someone is walking over before the engine has stopped ticking. Leave it among the Porsches and Ferraris at a cars-and-coffee and come back to a small crowd at its fenders, running their fingers along the slashes and arguing about what it is. Ray and Pauline Frost’s yellow 2005 car, nicknamed the Yellow Peril, has been photographed under the wing of a wartime Sea Hurricane fighter, and it looks perfectly at home there. It doesn’t resemble a Ferrari, a Lamborghini, a Porsche or even another TVR, and it can be recognized at once by people who have never seen one in person, a remarkable thing for a company that built a few hundred cars a year.

Rarity alone doesn’t make a car special, but the Sagaris had its own engine, chassis, design and interior, from a company that refused to share them, and it was built to reward skill rather than flatter the inexperienced. Modern sports cars are faster, safer and easier to drive quickly. The Sagaris is a reminder that driving can’t always be measured in lap times.

The final assignmentIf TVR had to go out

There is a wonderful symmetry in the way the Sagaris closes this chapter. It took something from every member of the family: not the Cerbera’s elegance, the Chimaera’s open air or the Tamora’s ease, but their ambition, their individuality and their belief that a sports car should make its driver feel something. It wasn’t the most practical TVR or the most forgiving, but it may have been the most complete expression of everything the company had been trying to achieve. That is what makes its story so bittersweet, because there is nothing sad about the car itself. It looks as though it has never once entertained the possibility of losing.

Imagine a quiet stretch of British countryside, the road twisting between the hedgerows toward the hills. Something approaches, and you hear it first: a hard-edged, mechanical howl that sounds far too urgent for a road car. Then it appears around the bend, low, wide and almost impossibly aggressive, its fenders slashed open and its hood rising and falling around those strange vents. It changes direction, the body settles, the driver feeds in the power, the engine climbs and the exhaust note sharpens, and the Sagaris disappears around the next bend with an urgency that makes you wonder whether you have just witnessed something entirely unreasonable. A few moments later, the sound fades, the road falls quiet, and you are left standing there, wondering what on earth that was.

That was TVR. Not the company at its biggest or most profitable, but perhaps the company at its most extraordinary. The Sagaris didn’t need to threaten, boast or pretend. Its looks made the introduction, its performance delivered the message and its handling made sure the job was done properly. It was the assassin. It was here for one thing, and you were it. And when the job was finished, it disappeared, leaving behind one of the most spectacular legacies of its generation. If TVR had to go out, at least it went out fighting.

If you want one

What they cost. The Classic Valuer puts the median Sagaris sale since 2020 at £64,695 ($85,800), with the best reaching £89,608 ($118,800). That is comfortably more than the £49,995 they cost new, although still less than that price in today’s money.

What to check. PistonHeads’ buying guide suggests servicing at 6,000-mile intervals and setting the valve clearances every 2 years or 12,000 miles. Look for leaking clutch slave cylinders, inspect the powder-coated chassis for any chip that could let water in, and test every electrical item, because the wiring behind the dashboard is prone to breaking.

In America. No Sagaris was sold new in the US, and the first production cars, delivered at the end of 2004, don’t turn 25 until the end of 2029. Start saving, and read The Long Road Home while you wait.

Some cars are built to be remembered. Others make certain you’ll never forget them.
